stem: Three moles of an ideal gas are expanded isothermally from 15 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) to 20 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) at constant external pressure of 1.2 bar. Estimate the amount of work in \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) bar and J.
solution:
\(W = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V = -P_{ext}\,(V_2 - V_1)\)
\(P_{ext} = 1.2\ \mathrm{bar}\), \(V_1 = 15\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), \(V_2 = 20\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)
Substitution of these quantities into the equation gives
\(W = -1.2\ \mathrm{bar}\,(20\ \mathrm{dm^3} - 15\ \mathrm{dm^3})\)
\(= -1.2\ \mathrm{bar} \times 5\ \mathrm{dm^3} = -6\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar}\)
\(1\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar} = 100\ \mathrm{J}\)
Hence, \(W = -6\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar} \times 100\ \mathrm{J/dm^3\ bar} = -600\ \mathrm{J}\)

stem: Calculate the constant external pressure required to compress 2 moles of an ideal gas from volume of 25 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) to 13 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) when the work obtained is 4862.4 J.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed working shows \(48.62\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar} = -P_{ext}(13\ \mathrm{dm^3} - 25\ \mathrm{dm^3}) = -P_{ext} \times 12\ \mathrm{dm^3}\). The second minus sign is wrong — \(-(13 - 25) = +12\) — and the book's own next line divides by \(+12\) to reach 4.052 bar. The sign has been corrected here so the derivation is self-consistent; the printed answer is unchanged.]

\(W = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V = -P_{ext}\,(V_2 - V_1)\)
\(V_1 = 25\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), \(V_2 = 13\ \mathrm{dm^3}\), \(W = 4862.4\ \mathrm{J}\)
\(W = 4862.4\ \mathrm{J} \times \dfrac{\mathrm{dm^3\ bar}}{100\ \mathrm{J}} = 48.62\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar}\)
Substitution of these into the equation gives
\(48.62\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar} = -P_{ext}\,(13\ \mathrm{dm^3} - 25\ \mathrm{dm^3}) = P_{ext} \times 12\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)
Hence, \(P_{ext} = \dfrac{48.62\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar}}{12\ \mathrm{dm^3}} = 4.052\ \mathrm{bar}\)

stem:
200 mL ethylene gas and 150 mL of HCl gas were allowed to react at 1 bar pressure according to the reaction
\(\mathrm{C_2H_4(g) + HCl(g) \longrightarrow C_2H_5Cl(g)}\)
Calculate the \(PV\) work in joules.
solution:
\(W = -P_{ext}\,\Delta V = -P_{ext}\,(V_2 - V_1)\)
According to the equation of reaction 1 mole of \(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\) reacts with 1 mole of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) to produce 1 mole of \(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl}\). Hence, 150 mL of \(\mathrm{HCl}\) would react with only 150 mL of \(\mathrm{C_2H_4}\) to produce 150 mL of \(\mathrm{C_2H_5Cl}\).
\(V_1 = 150\ \mathrm{mL} + 150\ \mathrm{mL} = 300\ \mathrm{mL} = 0.3\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)
\(V_2 = 150\ \mathrm{mL} = 0.15\ \mathrm{L}\), \(P_{ext} = 1\ \mathrm{bar}\)
Substitution of these quantities in above
\(W = -1\ \mathrm{bar}\,(0.15\ \mathrm{dm^3} - 0.3\ \mathrm{dm^3})\)
\(= 0.15\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar}\)
\(= 0.15\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar} \times 100\ \dfrac{\mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{dm^3\ bar}}\)
\(= 15.0\ \mathrm{J}\)

stem: 2 moles of an ideal gas are expanded isothermally and reversibly from 20 L to 30 L at 300 K. Calculate the work done (\(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\))
solution:
\(W_{max} = -2.303\,nRT \log_{10} \dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\)
\(n = 2\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(T = 300\ \mathrm{K}\), \(V_1 = 20\ \mathrm{L}\), \(V_2 = 30\ \mathrm{L}\), \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J/K\ mol}\)
Substitution of these quantities into the equation gives
\(W_{max} = -2.303 \times 2\ \mathrm{mol} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J/K\ mol} \times 300\ \mathrm{K} \times \log_{10} \dfrac{30\ \mathrm{L}}{20\ \mathrm{L}}\)
\(= -2.303 \times 2 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J} \times 300 \times \log_{10} 1.5\)
\(= -2.303 \times 2 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J} \times 300 \times 0.1761\)
\(= -2023\ \mathrm{J} = -2.023\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

stem: 22 g of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) are compressed isothermally and reversibly at 298 K from initial pressure of 100 kPa when the work obtained is 1.2 kJ. Find the final pressure.
solution:
\(W = -2.303\,nRT \log_{10} \dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\)
\(n = \dfrac{22\ \mathrm{g}}{44\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}} = 0.5\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\),
\(P_1 = 100\ \mathrm{kPa}\), \(W = 1.2\ \mathrm{kJ} = 1200\ \mathrm{J}\)
Hence, \(1200\ \mathrm{J} = -2.303 \times 0.5\ \mathrm{mol} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K} \times \log_{10} \dfrac{100\ \mathrm{kPa}}{P_2}\)
or \(\log_{10} \dfrac{100\ \mathrm{kPa}}{P_2} = \dfrac{-1200}{2.303 \times 0.5 \times 8.314 \times 298} = -0.4206\)
\(\dfrac{100\ \mathrm{kPa}}{P_2} = \mathrm{antilog}\,(-0.4206) = 0.3797\)
Therefore, \(P_2 = \dfrac{100\ \mathrm{kPa}}{0.3797} = 263.4\ \mathrm{kPa}\)

stem: 300 mmol of an ideal gas occupies 13.7 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) at 300 K. Calculate the work done when the gas is expanded until its volume has increased by 2.3 \(\mathrm{dm^3}\) (a) isothermally against a constant external pressure of 0.3 bar (b) isothermally and reversibly (c) into vacuum.
solution:
a. \(W = -P_{ex}\,\Delta V\)
\(P_{ext} = 0.3\ \mathrm{bar}\), \(\Delta V = 2.3\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)
\(W = -0.3\ \mathrm{bar} \times 2.3\ \mathrm{dm^3}\)
\(= -0.69\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar}\)
\(= -0.69\ \mathrm{dm^3\ bar} \times \dfrac{100\ \mathrm{J}}{\mathrm{dm^3\ bar}}\)
\(= -69\ \mathrm{J}\)

b. \(W_{max} = -2.303\,nRT \log_{10} \dfrac{V_2}{V_1}\)
\(n = 300\ \mathrm{mmol} = 300 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{mol} = 0.3\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(T = 300\ \mathrm{K}\)
\(W_{max} = -2.303 \times 0.3\ \mathrm{mol} \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}} \times 300\ \mathrm{K} \times \log_{10} \dfrac{16}{13.7}\)
\(= -2.303 \times 0.3 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J} \times 300 \times 0.0674\)
\(= -116.1\ \mathrm{J}\)

c. \(W = -P_{ex}\,\Delta V\)
When gas is expanded to vaccum, \(P_{ext} = 0\) and \(W = 0\)

subtopic: Enthalpy and Enthalpies of Physical Transformations
stem:
\(\Delta H\) for the reaction,
\(\mathrm{2C(s) + 3H_2(g) \longrightarrow C_2H_6(g)}\) is \(-84.4\) kJ at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\). Calculate \(\Delta U\) for the reaction at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\). (\(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\))
solution:
\(\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT\)
\(\Delta n_g\) = (moles of product gases) - (moles of reactant gases)
\(\Delta n_g = 1 - 3 = -2\ \mathrm{mol}\)
\(\Delta H = -84.4\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(= 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}}\)
Substitution of these in above
\(-84.4\ \mathrm{kJ} = \Delta U + 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K} \times (-2\ \mathrm{mol})\)
\(= \Delta U - 4.96\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
Hence, \(\Delta U = -84.4\ \mathrm{kJ} + 4.96\ \mathrm{kJ} = -79.44\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

stem: In a particular reaction 2 kJ of heat is released by the system and 6 kJ of work is done on the system. Determine of \(\Delta H\) and \(\Delta U\)?
solution:
According to the first law of thermodynamics
\(\Delta U = Q + W\)
\(Q = -2\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(W = +6\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
\(\Delta U = -2\ \mathrm{kJ} + 6\ \mathrm{kJ} = +4\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
\(Q_p = \Delta H = -2\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

subtopic: Enthalpy and Enthalpies of Physical Transformations
stem:
Calculate the work done in oxidation of 4 moles of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\) if
\(\mathrm{2\,SO_2(g) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,SO_3(g)}\)
\(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\)
State whether work is done on the system or by the system.
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book's printed working ends "\(= 4955\ \mathrm{J} = 4.955\ \mathrm{J}\)", a false equality — 4955 J is 4.955 kJ, not 4.955 J. The unit has been corrected here; the value 4955 J and the conclusion that work is done on the system are as printed.]

For oxidation of 4 moles of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\), the reaction is
\(\mathrm{4\,SO_2(g) + 2\,O_2(g) \longrightarrow 4\,SO_3(g)}\)
\(W = -\Delta n_g RT\)
\(\Delta n_g = 4 - 6 = -2\ \mathrm{mol}\), \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\)
Hence,
\(W = -2\ \mathrm{mol} \times -8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K}\)
\(= 4955\ \mathrm{J} = 4.955\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
Work is done on the system (since \(W > 0\)).

stem:
Calculate standard enthalpy of reaction,
\(\mathrm{2C_2H_6(g) + 7O_2(g) \longrightarrow 4\,CO_2(g) + 6\,H_2O(\mathit{l})}\)
Given that
\(\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{CO_2}) = -393.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\),
\(\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{H_2O}) = -285.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) and
\(\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{C_2H_6}) = -84.9\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)
solution:
\(\Delta_r H^0 = \sum \Delta_f H^0(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta_f H^0(\text{reactants})\)
\(= [4\,\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{CO_2}) + 6\,\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{H_2O})]\)
\(\qquad - [2\,\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{C_2H_6}) + 7\,\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{O_2})]\)
\(= [4\ \mathrm{mol} \times (-393.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}) + 6\ \mathrm{mol} \times (-285.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}})]\)
\(\qquad - [2\ \mathrm{mol} \times (-84.9\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}) + 0]\)
\(= -1574\ \mathrm{kJ} - 1714.8\ \mathrm{kJ} + 169.8\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
\(= -3119\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

stem: Estimate the standard enthalpy of combustion of \(\mathrm{CH_4(g)}\) if \(\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{CH_4}) = -74.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), \(\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{CO_2}) = -393.5\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) and \(\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{H_2O}) = -285.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)
solution:
The equation for the combustion of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) is
\(\mathrm{CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) \longrightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O(\mathit{l})}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = ?\)
\(\Delta_r H^0 = [\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{CO_2}) + 2\,\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{H_2O})]\)
\(\qquad - [\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{CH_4}) + 2\,\Delta_f H^0(\mathrm{O_2})]\)
\(= [1 \times (-393.5) + 2 \times (-285.8)]\)
\(\qquad - [1 \times (-74.8) + 2 \times 0]\)
\(\Delta_c H^0(\mathrm{CH_4}) = -890.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

Showing the bonds broken and formed,
\(\mathrm{H_2N-NH_2(g) + H-H(g) \longrightarrow 2\,NH_3(g)}\)
\(\Delta_r H^0 = \sum \Delta H^0(\text{reactant}) - \sum \Delta H^0(\text{product})\)
\(= [4\Delta H^0(\mathrm{N\text{-}H}) + \Delta H^0(\mathrm{N\text{-}N}) + \Delta H^0(\mathrm{H\text{-}H})] - [6\,\Delta H^0(\mathrm{N\text{-}H})]\)
\(= \Delta H^0(\mathrm{N\text{-}N}) + \Delta H^0(\mathrm{H\text{-}H}) - 2\,\Delta H^0(\mathrm{N\text{-}H})\)
\(= 1 \times 159 + 1\ \mathrm{mol} \times 435 - 2 \times 389\)
\(= -184\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

stem:
The enthalpy change of the following reaction
\(\mathrm{CH_4(g) + Cl_2(g) \longrightarrow CH_3Cl(g) + HCl(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -104\) kJ. Calculate C-Cl bond enthalpy. The bond enthalpies are

| Bond | C-H | Cl-Cl | H-Cl |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\Delta H^0/\mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) | 414 | 243 | 431 |
solution:
\(\Delta_r H^0 = \sum \Delta H^0(\text{reactant}) - \sum \Delta H^0(\text{product})\)
\(= [4\Delta H^0(\mathrm{C\text{-}H}) + \Delta H^0(\mathrm{Cl\text{-}Cl})] - [3\Delta H^0(\mathrm{C\text{-}H}) + \Delta H^0(\mathrm{C\text{-}Cl}) + \Delta H^0(\mathrm{H\text{-}Cl})]\)
\(= \Delta H^0(\mathrm{C\text{-}H}) + \Delta H^0(\mathrm{Cl\text{-}Cl}) - \Delta H^0(\mathrm{C\text{-}Cl}) - \Delta H^0(\mathrm{H\text{-}Cl})\)
\(-104\ \mathrm{kJ} = 1 \times 414 + 1 \times 243 - 1 \times \Delta H^0(\mathrm{C\text{-}Cl}) - 1 \times 431\)
\(= 226 - 1 \times \Delta H^0(\mathrm{C\text{-}Cl})\)
\(1 \times \Delta H^0(\mathrm{C\text{-}Cl}) = 226 + 104\)
\(\Delta H^0(\mathrm{C\text{-}Cl}) = 330\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem:
Calculate the standard enthalpy of the reaction,
\(\mathrm{2Fe(s) + \tfrac{3}{2}\,O_2(g) \longrightarrow Fe_2O_3(s)}\)
Given :
i. \(\mathrm{2Al(s) + Fe_2O_3(s) \longrightarrow 2Fe(s) + Al_2O_3(s)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -847.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
ii. \(\mathrm{2\,Al(s) + \tfrac{3}{2}\,O_2(g) \longrightarrow Al_2O_3(s)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -1670\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
solution:
Reverse Eq.(i) and then add to Eq. (ii)
\(\mathrm{2Fe(s) + Al_2O_3(s) \longrightarrow 2\,Al(s) + Fe_2O_3(s)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = +847.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
\(\mathrm{2\,Al(s) + \tfrac{3}{2}\,O_2(g) \longrightarrow Al_2O_3(s)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -1670\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

\(\mathrm{2Fe(s) + \tfrac{3}{2}\,O_2(g) \longrightarrow Fe_2O_3(s)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -822.4\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

stem:
Calculate the standard enthalpy of the reaction,
\(\mathrm{SiO_2(s) + 3C(graphite) \longrightarrow SiC(s) + 2\,CO(g)}\)
from the following reactions,
i. \(\mathrm{Si(s) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow SiO_2(s)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -911\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
ii. \(\mathrm{2\,C(graphite) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow 2CO(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -221\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
iii. \(\mathrm{Si(s) + C(graphite) \longrightarrow SiC(s)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -65.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the book prints the reversed equation (iv) first as \(\Delta_r H^0 = -911\) kJ and then, four lines later, correctly as \(+911\) kJ. Reversing equation (i) must flip the sign, so \(+911\) kJ is right and the first printing is a misprint; it has been corrected here. Note also that the three values summed give \(-221 - 65.3 + 911 = +624.7\) kJ, which the book rounds to \(+624\) kJ.]

Reverse the Eq. (i)
iv. \(\mathrm{SiO_2(s) \longrightarrow Si(s) + O_2(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = +911\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
Add equations (ii), (iii) and (iv)
ii. \(\mathrm{2\,C(graphite) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow 2\,CO(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -221\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
iii. \(\mathrm{Si(s) + C(graphite) \longrightarrow SiC(s)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = -65.3\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
iv. \(\mathrm{SiO_2(s) \longrightarrow Si(s) + O_2(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = +911\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

\(\mathrm{SiO_2(s) + 3\,C(graphite) \longrightarrow SiC(s) + 2\,CO(g)}\), \(\Delta_r H^0 = +624\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

stem:
State whether following reactions are spontaneous or not. Further state whether they are exothermic or endothermic.
a. \(\Delta H = -110\ \mathrm{kJ}\) and \(\Delta S = +40\ \mathrm{JK^{-1}}\) at 400 K
b. \(\Delta H = +50\ \mathrm{kJ}\) and \(\Delta S = -130\ \mathrm{JK^{-1}}\) at 250 K
solution:
a. \(\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S\)
\(\Delta H = -110\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(\Delta S = +40\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\)
\(= +40 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}}\), \(T = 400\ \mathrm{K}\)
Therefore, \(\Delta G = -110\ \mathrm{kJ} - 400\ \mathrm{K} \times 40 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}}\)
\(= -110\ \mathrm{kJ} - 16\ \mathrm{kJ} = -126\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
Since \(\Delta G\) is negative, the reaction is spontaneous. It is exothermic since \(\Delta H\) is negative

b. \(\Delta H = +50\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(\Delta S = -130\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\)
\(= -130 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}}\), \(T = 250\ \mathrm{K}\)
\(\Delta G = +50\ \mathrm{kJ} - 250\ \mathrm{K} \times (-130 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}})\)
\(= 50\ \mathrm{kJ} + 32.5\ \mathrm{kJ} = +82.5\ \mathrm{kJ}\)
As \(\Delta G\) is positive, the reaction is nonspontaneous. It is endothermic since \(\Delta H\) is positive.

stem: For a certain reaction \(\Delta H^0\) is \(-224\) kJ and \(\Delta S^0\) is \(-153\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\). At what temperature the change over from spontaneous to nonspontaneous will occur?
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the substitution is printed as \(T = \dfrac{-224\ \mathrm{kJ}}{-0.153\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}}\). The denominator should read \(\mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}}\) — the line immediately above converts \(-153\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\) to \(-0.153\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}}\) precisely so that it matches the numerator. It is preserved as printed; the value 1464 K is correct.]

\(T = \dfrac{\Delta H^0}{\Delta S^0}\)
\(\Delta H^0 = -224\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(\Delta S^0 = -153\ \mathrm{JK^{-1}} = -0.153\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}}\)
Therefore, \(T = \dfrac{-224\ \mathrm{kJ}}{-0.153\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}} = +1464\ \mathrm{K}\)
Since \(\Delta H^0\) and \(\Delta S^0\) are both negative, the reaction is spontaneous at low temperatures. A change over will occur at 1464 K. The reaction is spontaneous below 1464 K.

stem:
For the reaction,
\(\mathrm{CH_4(g) + H_2(g) \longrightarrow C_2H_6(g)}\),
\(K_p = 3.356 \times 10^{17}\)
Calculate \(\Delta G^0\) for the reaction at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
solution:
[Textbook misprint: the reaction is printed as \(\mathrm{CH_4(g) + H_2(g) \longrightarrow C_2H_6(g)}\), which is not balanced — there is one carbon on the left and two on the right. The equation that balances and matches the hydrogen count is \(\mathrm{C_2H_4(g) + H_2(g) \longrightarrow C_2H_6(g)}\). It is preserved as printed because the calculation uses only \(K_p\), so the answer \(-100\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) is unaffected.]

\(\Delta G^0 = -2.303\,RT \log_{10} K_p\)
\(R = 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\), \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\),
\(K_p = 3.356 \times 10^{17}\)
\(\Delta G^0 = -2.303 \times 8.314 \times 298 \times \log_{10}(3.356 \times 10^{17})\)
\(= -2.303 \times 8.314\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}} \times 298 \times 17.526\)
\(= -100{,}000\ \mathrm{J\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(= -100\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)

stem:
Calculate \(\Delta S_{total}\) and state whether the reaction is spontaneous or nonspontaneous at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\).
\(\mathrm{HgS(s) + O_2(g) \longrightarrow Hg(\mathit{l}) + SO_2(g)}\),
\(\Delta H^0 = -238.6\ \mathrm{kJ}\), \(\Delta S^0 = +36.7\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\)
solution:
\(\Delta S_{surr} = -\dfrac{\Delta H^0}{T} = -\dfrac{(-238.6\ \mathrm{kJ})}{298\ \mathrm{K}}\)
\(= +0.8007\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}} = +800.7\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\)
\(\Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr}\)
\(= +36.7\ \mathrm{JK^{-1}} + 800.7\ \mathrm{JK^{-1}}\)
\(= +837.4\ \mathrm{J\ K^{-1}}\)
\(\Delta S_{total} > 0\), the reaction is spontaneous at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

stem:
Calculate \(\Delta G\) for the reaction at \(25^\circ\mathrm{C}\)
\(\mathrm{CO(g) + 2\,H_2(g) \longrightarrow CH_3OH(g)}\), \(\Delta G^0 = -24.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\) The partial pressures of gases are \(P_{CO} = 4\ \mathrm{bar}\), \(P_{H_2} = 2\ \mathrm{bar}\) and \(P_{CH_3OH} = 2\ \mathrm{bar}\)
solution:
\(\Delta G = \Delta G^0 + RT \ln Q_p\)
\(= \Delta G^0 + 2.303\,RT \log_{10} \dfrac{P_{CH_3OH}}{P_{CO} \times P^2_{H_2}}\)
\(\Delta G^0 = -24.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), \(R = 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}\,mol^{-1}}\), \(T = 298\ \mathrm{K}\)
Calculate \(Q_p\),
\(Q_p = \dfrac{P_{CH_3OH}}{P_{CO} \times P^2_{H_2}} = \dfrac{2}{4 \times 4} = \dfrac{1}{8} = 0.125\)
\(\Delta G = -24.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}} + 2.303 \times 8.314 \times 10^{-3}\ \mathrm{kJ\ K^{-1}\ mol^{-1}} \times 298\ \mathrm{K} \times \log_{10} 0.125\)
\(= -24.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}} + 5.706 \times (-0.903)\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(= -24.8\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}} - 5.153\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)
\(= -29.953\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\)
